newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Retired French general to meet Zairean rebel chief.
newsitem.headline: Retired French general to meet Zairean rebel chief.

text.p: A retired French general arrived in Zaire's second largest city of Lubumbashi on Wednesday for talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila, diplomats said.

They said general Jeannou Lacaze, a former chief of staff of the French armed forces, and another Frenchman, who was not identified, had arrived to meet Kabila, head of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire.
A French foreign ministry spokesman said Lacaze, a former defence ministry adviser on Africa, was visiting Lubumbashi in a private capacity and was not accompanied by a French diplomat.

Rebel officials confirmed the two men's presence but gave no details. "It is a secret visit. They are holding talks with the president (Kabila) and I am not authorised to give details," said an official in Kabila's office.
Kabila has repeatedly accused France, a long-term ally of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, of seeking to block a rebel victory in Africa's third largest country during seven months of fighting.
But France has started distancing itself from Mobutu and this week urged the rebels to seek a peaceful settlement to the war since October rather than carry out their threat to seize Kinshasa.
France says the formation of a transitional government in Zaire would mark the start of national reconciliation. But Kabila insists that Mobutu must hand over power to him directly.
U.N. and Organisation of African Unity special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun was in Paris on Tuesday for talks with officials at President Jacques Chirac's office and the foreign ministry.

"We strongly wish for an immediate halt to hostilities, as foreseen in the peace plan," he said. "In this regard, we view with deep concern the latest declarations by Mr Kabila indicating that he has not renounced the military option," said French foreign ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt.
Kabila has vowed to chase Mobutu out of Kinshasa unless he has handed over power by the time rebels arrive in the capital.
Rummelhardt said Paris fully backed appeals by the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, Sadako Ogata, to the rebels to let aid reach the needy and allow unrestricted repatriation of Rwandan refugees.

Some 300 French soldiers were among western troops standing by in Brazzaville, across the river from Kinshasa in Congo, to evacuate foreigners. They could be reinforced if necessary by French units in Gabon, the Central African Republic and Chad.
U.S. envoy Bill Richardson, who has shuttled between Zaire and regional countries in a bid to avert bloodshed in Kinshasa, left Cape Town for Paris on Wednesday to consult France.
Mobutu meanwhile flew from Kinshasa to Gabon's capital Libreville. Aides said he would attend a regional summit on efforts to broker peace in Zaire and would return home on Friday.
But his departure raised speculation in Kinshasa he had left for good.
